before.title: Calciphylaxis
before.diseaseDescription: Calciphylaxis (calcific uraemic arteriolopathy): ischaemic skin necrosis from calcification, intimal thickening and thrombosis of small cutaneous arterioles, mainly in people on dialysis. This bounded map covers dialysis and clinical risk factors (phosphate, calcium load, PTH, obesity, diabetes, corticosteroids, hypoalbuminaemia, female sex), calcification-inhibitor deficiency (vitamin K status, warfarin, matrix Gla protein, fetuin-A), vascular smooth-muscle osteogenic change, arteriolar calcification, thrombophilia and microthrombosis, skin necrosis, sepsis and mortality. Most human links are associations from case-control studies and biopsy series; causal links rest on rodent knockout/warfarin models and in vitro work. Contradicting and qualifying results are retained.

scientificSummary.scope: A bounded map of calcific uraemic arteriolopathy: mineral-metabolism drivers, calcification-inhibitor deficiency (MGP/vitamin K, fetuin-A), vascular smooth-muscle osteogenic change, arteriolar calcification, thrombosis and skin ischaemic necrosis, plus curated therapies.

paragraphs.text: This bounded calciphylaxis map centres on small-vessel calcification together with thrombosis and vascular narrowing in predominantly dialysis-related disease. Human studies associate disease with aspects of mineral metabolism, vitamin K antagonism and reduced calcification-inhibitor activity; cultured smooth-muscle-cell and animal experiments support mechanisms involving phosphate, matrix Gla protein and fetuin-A. Human skin studies link an osteogenic programme with arteriolar mineral deposition and show thrombosis/intimal hyperplasia in lesional skin. Endothelial culture experiments add an inflammatory tissue-factor route to coagulation. The resulting model proposes convergence of calcification and vascular occlusion rather than a sufficient explanation based on mineral deposition alone.

Risk-factor findings vary across cohorts: phosphate and parathyroid-hormone results are not uniform, and vascular calcification can occur in clinically normal skin. Observational associations and experimental vascular calcification should not be equated with proven human calciphylaxis causation. Treatment signals are also limited: CALCIPHYX did not meet its wound or pain primary endpoints, uncontrolled sodium-thiosulfate improvement reports do not establish efficacy, and the cited vitamin K trial improved a biomarker without reducing coronary calcification progression. A secondary cinacalcet prevention analysis does not establish treatment of existing lesions. This selected-report summary requires an independent current-literature check of the combined mechanism, important omissions and therapeutic interpretation.

paragraphs.text: This bounded calciphylaxis map centres on small-vessel calcification together with thrombosis and vascular narrowing in predominantly dialysis-related disease. Human studies associate disease with aspects of mineral metabolism, vitamin K antagonism and reduced calcification-inhibitor activity; cultured smooth-muscle-cell and animal experiments support mechanisms involving phosphate, matrix Gla protein and fetuin-A. Human skin studies link an osteogenic programme with arteriolar mineral deposition and show thrombosis/intimal hyperplasia in lesional skin. Endothelial culture experiments add an inflammatory tissue-factor route to coagulation. The resulting model proposes convergence of calcification and vascular occlusion rather than a sufficient explanation based on mineral deposition alone. A newly added human registry study found lower circulating pyrophosphate in 30 calciphylaxis cases than in 30 matched controls; in its 70-patient cohort, lower levels were also associated with higher short-term mortality. This adds an observational calcification-inhibitor signal without demonstrating that PPi deficiency causes calciphylaxis.

Risk-factor findings vary across cohorts: phosphate and parathyroid-hormone results are not uniform, and vascular calcification can occur in clinically normal skin. Observational associations and experimental vascular calcification should not be equated with proven human calciphylaxis causation. Treatment signals are also limited: CALCIPHYX did not meet its wound or pain primary endpoints, uncontrolled sodium-thiosulfate improvement reports do not establish efficacy, and the cited vitamin K trial improved a biomarker without reducing coronary calcification progression. A secondary cinacalcet prevention analysis does not establish treatment of existing lesions. The pyrophosphate study was small, industry-funded and observational, with substantial within-person variability; PPi did not correlate with pain intensity. Raising PPi was not tested, and no treatment benefit is inferred. This is a selected-report local candidate with pending domain review.

after.label: Circulating pyrophosphate
after.description: Circulating calcification inhibitor measured in a human calciphylaxis registry; lower levels were associated with case status and outcomes, without establishing causal deficiency.

after.text: In the calciphylaxis cohort, lower enrollment PPi was associated with higher short-term mortality; PPi also correlated with lesion count but not pain intensity. These observations do not establish that raising PPi improves outcomes.
limitations: Seventy-patient cohort, short follow-up, substantial within-person PPi variability and possible residual confounding.
The adjusted mortality association was reported in the ESKD subgroup; no universal mortality effect is asserted.
No significant association with pain intensity; biomarker association does not demonstrate treatment benefit.

after.text: Circulating pyrophosphate was lower in 30 patients with calciphylaxis than in 30 matched controls; lower PPi was associated with higher odds of calciphylaxis after adjustment for ALP, phosphate and BMI.
limitations: Small observational matched case-control study; measurement after diagnosis cannot establish temporal direction or causation.
Only 67% had ESKD; findings must not be treated as a dialysis-only population.
Industry funded, with several authors employed by the sponsor. No PPi-raising intervention was tested.
